context: The opening prayer of the Quran, recited in every unit of prayer, asking for guidance on the straight path.
The longest surah; lays out law, worship, patience and the stories of earlier prophets for the new Medinan community.
Continues themes from Al-Baqarah, centers on the family of Imran and discussions with Christians and Jews after the Battle of Badr.
Lays out rules for family life, inheritance, and justice, named for its emphasis on the rights of women.
The last major legal surah revealed, includes the story of the Last Supper-like table and completes core rulings.
A sweeping Meccan surah arguing for God's oneness through nature, reason and the fate of earlier nations.
Recounts the stories of Adam, Noah, and several prophets rejected by their peoples, warning Mecca of a similar fate.
Reflects on the Battle of Badr, the first major victory of the early Muslim community, and the ethics of war.
The only surah without an opening Bismillah, addressing treaties, hypocrisy and the final shape of the early Muslim state.
Named after the prophet Jonah, defends the reality of revelation and the resurrection against Meccan skeptics.
Retells several prophetic stories including Noah, Hud, and Lot, each ending in their people's downfall.
Tells the single continuous story of Joseph, his betrayal by his brothers, and his rise in Egypt.
Reflects on thunder as a sign of God's power, and on the patience required of those who believe.
Named for the prophet Abraham, contrasts gratitude and ingratitude using the parable of a good and a bad tree.
Named after a sandy valley wiped out for rejecting a prophet; reaffirms the Quran's protection from distortion.
Known as 'The Bee', surveys the natural world as evidence of a single creator and provider.
Opens with the Prophet's night journey, then lays out a concise code of ethics for daily life.
Contains four parables — the Cave, the two gardens, Moses and al-Khidr, and Dhul-Qarnayn — about wealth, knowledge and time.
Named after Mary, tells of the births of John and Jesus and affirms Jesus's place as a prophet, not divine.
Tells the story of Moses from his calling at the burning bush through his confrontation with Pharaoh.
Surveys many prophets briefly, stressing that each was sent with the same core message despite different peoples.
Covers the rites of pilgrimage alongside permission to defend the early community against persecution.
Describes the qualities of successful believers and the stages of human creation as signs of design.
Best known for its guidance on modesty and the account that cleared Aisha of slander, known as 'The Light'.
Called 'The Criterion', answers objections to the Prophet's mission and contrasts the righteous with the heedless.
Retells the stories of Moses, Abraham, Noah, Lot, and others, each confronting a people who denied them.
Centers on Solomon, the Queen of Sheba, and the wonders given to him, named for the ant parable within it.
Tells the fuller story of Moses's early life, exile to Madyan, and the tyranny of Pharaoh and Qarun.
Named for the spider's fragile web, used as an image for misplaced trust in anything besides God.
Opens by predicting Rome's recovery over Persia, then turns to signs of God in creation and the human soul.
Named after a wise, non-prophetic figure whose advice to his son models humility and gratitude.
A short surah on the Day of Judgment, contrasting the fate of the devoted and the arrogant.
Addresses events around the Battle of the Trench and sets out norms for the Prophet's household and community.
Named after David, recounts the favors shown to David and Solomon and warns against taking blessings for granted.
Called 'The Originator', reflects on God as creator and sustainer of the natural order.
Often recited for the dying or departed, affirms resurrection and the Quran's message through vivid imagery.
Describes ranks of angels in worship and retells the stories of Noah, Abraham, and Jonah as examples of faith.
Named after the Arabic letter Saad, recounts David's repentance and Solomon's trials as models of humility in power.
Called 'The Throngs', depicts people being gathered in groups on Judgment Day according to how they lived.
Named for a believer in Pharaoh's court who argued for mercy toward Moses, modeling quiet courage.
Begins a series of surahs opened with 'Ha Mim', inviting careful reflection on the Quran's clarity.
Discusses consultation and mutual counsel as a value for believers, alongside the themes of revelation and patience.
Named after ornamental gold, questions the value placed on wealth and lineage over guidance.
Describes a thick smoke as one image of the coming judgment, recalling Pharaoh's downfall as a precedent.
Named 'The Kneeling', pictures every community kneeling before its record on the Day of Judgment.
Named after shifting sand dunes, reflects on the generations that lived and vanished before the present one.
Addresses the conduct and purpose of the believers in conflict, named for the image of Muhammad as their leader.
Reflects on a peace treaty (Hudaybiyyah) that looked like a setback but opened the way for later success.
Sets out etiquette among believers — verifying news, avoiding suspicion, and treating one another with respect.
Named after the Arabic letter Qaf, affirms resurrection against those who found the idea implausible.
Named for the winds that scatter, uses natural imagery to argue for an ordered, purposeful universe.
Named after Mount Sinai, defends the authenticity of revelation against accusations made by skeptics.
Describes a vision experienced by the Prophet and criticizes the worship of lesser deities alongside God.
Named 'The Moon', recalls the destruction of several ancient peoples as warnings repeated throughout history.
Known as 'The Merciful', lists pairs of blessings with the refrain asking which can be denied.
Describes three groups on Judgment Day — the foremost, the companions of the right, and those of the left.
Named 'Iron', encourages charitable spending and reflects on faith as something that should soften the heart.
Named for a woman who pleaded her case before the Prophet, setting rules protecting women within marriage.
Reflects on the exile of a tribe from Medina and sets principles for distributing communal gains.

meaning: She that is to be examined
context: Sets guidance on relations with those outside the faith, distinguishing hostility from ordinary coexistence.
Named 'The Ranks', calls believers to stand firm together, drawing a comparison to a solid structure.
Named for the Friday congregational prayer, emphasizing community and setting aside worldly distraction for it.
Describes the behavior of those who outwardly conform but inwardly withhold sincerity.
Named 'Mutual Loss and Gain', reflects on how this life's choices carry into the next.
Sets out practical rules for divorce and the waiting period that follows it.
Addresses an episode in the Prophet's household, using it to speak more broadly about repentance and resolve.
Known as 'The Dominion', reflects on God's control over creation as a basis for humility and trust.
Named after the pen, defends the Prophet's character against accusations made by his contemporaries.
Describes the Day of Judgment arriving as an undeniable, inescapable reality.
Named 'The Ways of Ascent', contrasts human impatience with the long timescale of divine justice.
Retells Noah's long effort to call his people and their refusal to listen.
Describes a group of jinn who, upon hearing the Quran recited, were moved to believe.
Named for the Prophet wrapped in a cloak, instructs him to rise for night prayer in preparation for his mission.
Continues the address to the Prophet, urging him to warn his people and persevere under pressure.
Named 'The Resurrection', argues for the plausibility of being raised again after death.
Describes the reward awaiting those who give to others despite their own need.
Repeats the refrain 'woe to the deniers' across a series of warnings about the Day of Judgment.
Opens a run of short, rhythmic surahs describing the natural world and the events of the Last Day.
Describes angels tasked with the resurrection, and recalls Pharaoh's confrontation with Moses as a cautionary tale.
Begins with a gentle correction of the Prophet over how he treated a visitor, stressing humility toward all.
Known as 'The Overturning', uses striking cosmic imagery for the unraveling of the world at its end.
Named 'The Cleaving', pictures the sky splitting apart as part of the Day of Judgment's imagery.
Condemns those who cheat in weighing and measuring, tying everyday honesty to accountability before God.
Named 'The Splitting', describes the earth and sky yielding up everything they hold on the Last Day.
Recalls the persecution of early believers burned for their faith, affirming that patience under trial is not wasted.
Named after the night star, affirms the Quran's truth with an oath by the clear sky.
Known as 'The Most High', praises God as creator and sustainer who makes growth and renewal possible.
Describes two overturning scenes — a bleak one and a pleasant one — depicting the opposite outcomes of judgment.
Named 'The Dawn', reflects on the rise and fall of past civilizations as a lesson on power and humility.
Named 'The City', reflects on human struggle and the two paths of ease or difficulty one can choose.
Named 'The Sun', ties the soul's success to self-discipline, telling the story of a people destroyed for cruelty to an animal.
Named 'The Night', contrasts generosity with miserliness as two opposite responses to what one is given.
Named 'The Morning Light', reassures the Prophet during a period of silence in revelation that he was not abandoned.
Known as 'The Opening Up', reminds the Prophet that relief follows hardship.
Named 'The Fig', reflects on human dignity and the responsibility that comes with it.
Traditionally held to be the first revelation, it commands reading and learning in God's name.
Named 'The Night of Decree', describes the night the Quran's revelation began as better than a thousand months.
Named 'The Clear Proof', distinguishes sincere belief from mere inherited tradition.
Named 'The Earthquake', describes the earth testifying to everything that happened on it on the Last Day.
Named 'The Chargers', uses the image of galloping horses to question human ingratitude.
Named 'The Calamity', describes the Day of Judgment as an event that shakes every certainty.
Named 'Rivalry in Increase', warns against being consumed by the pursuit of more.
Named 'Time', a brief surah holding that only faith, good deeds, and mutual encouragement in truth save a person from loss.
Named 'The Slanderer', criticizes those who hoard wealth and belittle others.
Named 'The Elephant', recalls an army's failed attack on Mecca as a sign of protection.
Named after the Quraysh tribe, calls on them to be grateful to the one who secured their trade routes.
Named 'Small Kindnesses', ties sincere worship to caring for orphans and those in need.
Named 'Abundance', a short surah of comfort promising the Prophet abundant good in response to his critics.
Named 'The Disbelievers', draws a clear line between one's own faith and that of others, without hostility.
Named 'Victory', understood as marking the Prophet's mission nearing its completion.
Named after an uncle of the Prophet who opposed him, an early example of consequence for persistent hostility.
Named 'Sincerity', a short, dense statement of God's absolute oneness, often described as a concise creed.
Named 'The Daybreak', a short prayer for protection from harm, envy and hidden evil.
Named 'Mankind', closes the Quran with a prayer for protection from inward whispers of harm.
